newsitem.title: USA: GFOA panel adopts mark-up rules, litigation reform.
newsitem.headline: GFOA panel adopts mark-up rules, litigation reform.

text.p: The Government Finance Officers Association's executive board on Monday voted to urge NASD to adopt mark-up rules for the government securities market, including a requirement that dealers disclose price mark-ups upon request before completion of a sale.
The board adopted that and 11 other policy statements that had been approved by GFOA committees over the weekend.
GFOA's full membership, which is meeting here for the group's 91st annual conference, is expected to approve the 12 policy statements on Tuesday.
The board also cleared a policy opposing new litigation and regulation reform efforts on Capitol Hill that would preempt state securities laws and limit access to state courts by bond buyers.

"GFOA opposes federal efforts to preempt state laws regulating investments and securities transactions ... and limit access or remedies provided by state courts for defrauded public investors seeking recovery," the draft policy says.
The draft policy drew objections from one GFOA member on Saturday who said he is "disturbed" by a bondholders' lawsuit against the city of Denver.

The city and bond dealers last week announced a $4.1 million dollar settlement of the lawsuit which challenged the quality of disclosure in bond documents for the sale of Denver International Airport bonds.
"There are several questions that this committee needs to ask about what happened," Frank Hoadley, a member of GFOA's governmental debt committee said on Saturday.

Hoadley wondered whether the lawsuit was triggered in part by Securities and Exchange Commission Chairman Arthur Levitt's aggressive enforcement strategy in munis, including a probe of the Denver bonds.
The agency had gone so far as issuing a so-called "Wells" letter to Denver asking why it should not bring enforcement action promptly. It later notified Denver it was dropping the investigation.

"What effect did the Wells letter have on" the decision by bondholders to sue in the first place, asked Hoadley, capital finance director for the state of Wisconsin. He also asked whether SEC's 1994 municipal disclosure Rule 15c2-12 has triggered an increase in issuer liability.

Catherine Spain, head of GFOA's federal liaison center, told Hoadley at Saturday's meeting that the governmental debt committee will look into his concerns. She added, however, that the committee has stated clearly that it opposes frivolous lawsuits.

Another policy cleared on Monday calls for a joint effort by municiapl groups to develop and implement uniform practices for getting important default notices to actual bondholders, known as "beneficial" owners. Because of book-entry registration, many notices currently go only to nominal holders of bonds.
One draft policy opposes federal legislation that would relax standards for exchange-traded derivatives and that would create a "professional trading market" for futures.
Two other board policies would encourage governments to remove "artificial restrictions" on the investment of public funds and the use of banking services.
Other policies would:
* Oppose legislation that fails to preserve the right of state and local governments to enact and administer their own tax laws without federal preemption.
* Support the use of the cooperative purchasing program administered by the General Services Administration by state and local governments.
* Support efforts to modify federal restrictions on the amount of contributions that may be paid to a qualified pension plan during a 12-month period.

The panel also cleared policies concerning pension "portability," permanent extension of the U.S. tax code's education assistance exclusion, public pension plan investments and deferred compensation plans.
--Vicky Stamas, 202-898-8314
